title: 'lcm-closed' solutions (x | z): fail only at 2521 among all primes ≤ 10⁵ and all n ≤ 3000
connection: Solutions with x | z (equivalently y | z in the data: identical failure set and share 0.377) exist for every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, the hardest ES prime; none of the 9 solutions of 4/2521 has x | z.
why: A sub-family with a single exception ≤ 10⁵ — and the exception is the extremal 'all small primes split' prime. 4/p = (a + b + 1)/z with a, b | z is a pure 'three divisors of z summing to 4z/p' problem: a practical-number style formulation.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷; test whether failures are exactly primes ≡ 1 (mod lcm(1..k)) with k large; prove x | z ⟺ y | z for prime n.

title: Graph covers and congruence refinement
connection: View reduction modulo a larger modulus as a refinement of a smaller residue-state graph.
why: Covering-like behavior could make iterative modular analysis systematic; exceptional fibers are equally informative.
first_step: Compare transition graphs modulo 4 and 8 and classify how vertices and edges lift.

title: Hypergraph Turán / Erdős–Ko–Rado: the family of 'divisor sets in class' as an intersecting family
connection: Fix p. For each C, S_C = divisors of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. The family {S_C} over C — are the sets pairwise 'related' (e.g. a divisor a of 4Cp+1 and a' of 4C'p+1 have gcd structure: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | (C − C')·4p... so gcd divides 4(C' − C))? That bounds how much two S_C can overlap — an 'almost disjointness' that makes the counting cleaner.
why: Near-disjointness of the certificate sets across C means the total count Σ|S_C| has small variance from overlaps — relevant to the second-moment approach and to 'at least one is nonempty' bookkeeping.
first_step: Prove gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | 4(C−C')·… precisely; then the divisors in S_C ∩ S_{C'} are ≤ 4|C − C'| — tiny. Record the lemma.

title: Convolution-on-group view: the divisor multiset of N mod 4C is a multiset D ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^×; certificates = D ∋ −1; D = product-set of the prime-power 'intervals' {1, q, …, q^e} — a Minkowski product of 'geometric progressions' in the group; Kneser's theorem bounds |D| from below
connection: |D| ≥ Σ (|D_q| − 1) + 1 (Cauchy–Davenport analogue for abelian groups via Kneser) when there is no stabiliser; so with ω(N) factors, |D| ≥ ω + 1 roughly — tiny versus φ(4C). Kneser's theorem also says: if |D| is small then D is a union of cosets of a subgroup H (periodic) — then −1 ∈ D iff the coset structure includes it: a *structural* dichotomy: either D is large (random-like, then −1 ∈ D with 'probability' |D|/φ) or D is periodic with stabiliser H (then −1 ∈ D ⟺ −1 ∈ D·H, a subgroup question). This is a rigorous version of the 'subgroup vs subset-product' gap.
why: Kneser's structure theorem is a real theorem applicable pointwise (at each (p, C)); it reorganises failures into 'small non-periodic D' (few factors — the dominant failure mode) vs 'periodic D missing −1' (subgroup obstruction).
first_step: For (p, C) failures, compute D, its stabiliser H = {h : hD = D}, and classify; check the Kneser bound tightness.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0268] Apply Kneser iteratively to the divisor sets of consecutive slices pooled in one group (common e) and record stabiliser chains.
[upgrades-0128] For hard primes and C ≤ 100 compute |product set|/φ(4C) and the Kneser stabiliser; classify failures.
refs: Kneser, Abschätzung der asymptotischen Dichte von Summenmengen, Math. Z. 58 (1953)

title: Rich-failure structure: when ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 and −1 ∉ D, is D ⊂ H for an index-2 subgroup H (i.e. all prime factors lie in the kernel of one odd character)?
connection: Kneser-periodic failures with nontrivial stabiliser; the simplest is 'all factors in ker χ for an odd χ'. If rich failures are ALWAYS of this form, then: ES(p) fails ⟹ for every C with rich 4Cp+1 there is an odd character χ_C mod 4C with χ_C(q) = 1 for all q | 4Cp+1 — i.e. 4Cp+1 is a 'norm' from the quadratic field of χ_C. Then 4Cp+1 ∈ N(K_C) for every rich C — a family of 'simultaneous norm' conditions on linear forms in C, controlled by half-dimensional sieves over C (pointwise in p!): #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} — but K_C varies with C, so the sieve is over a varying family; still each condition has 'density 1/√log' heuristically and the expected number of C ≤ X satisfying it is X/√log X ≪ X — but we need to show it's < (number of rich C), i.e. that NOT ALL rich C are norms, which requires the sieve LOWER bound… no: we need an upper bound on #{C: 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} < #{rich C} ≈ X. An upper bound ≪ X/√log X·const would suffice for X large! The catch: uniformity in p and the varying K_C. Promising structure. [CHECKED after writing: FALSE as a dichotomy — for p < 6000, C < 150, among 4182 failures with Ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 5, only 1651 (39%) have factors generating a −1-free subgroup; in 61% the factors generate −1 but no subset product equals −1 (multiplicity poverty). So the norm-type sieve bounds only ~40% of rich failures; the remaining gap is the Davenport-constant regime described two items below.]
why: If the dichotomy holds empirically and the sieve upper bound is provable uniformly, this is a *pointwise* proof sketch: 'poor C are few (Turán–Kubilius), norm-type C are few (half-dimensional sieve over varying fields), so some C is rich and non-norm ⟹ its subset-product set is non-periodic and large... ⟹ contains −1?' — the last step is the gap (large non-periodic D need not contain −1). Needs Kneser + a counting argument: |D| ≥ ω + 1 is too weak; but for non-periodic D the Kneser/Kemperman structure might force |D| ≥ φ(4C)/2 + 1 (if D·D ⊂ D-like); then D ∪ (−D) covers the group... −1 ∈ D ⟺ 1 ∈ −D; hmm, D is a product set containing 1; −1 ∈ D iff... Let me record the chain and its gap honestly.
first_step: (1) Empirically test the 'rich failure ⟹ all factors in ker of one odd χ' claim for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 300. (2) If it holds, write the sieve upper bound for #{C ≤ X : all prime factors of 4Cp+1 in ker χ_C for SOME odd χ_C mod 4C} with explicit uniformity. (3) Identify the exact gap between 'rich, non-norm' and '−1 ∈ D'.

title: Zero-sum theory (EGZ, Davenport) cannot be applied by pooling prime factors across C — B2 in zero-sum language
connection: Zero-sum / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv flavour: with multiplicities, the prime factors of Π_{C ≤ K} (4Cp+1) (pooled across C!) form a long sequence in… different groups (ℤ/4C)^× — no common group. But pooled across C with 4C | M for a fixed M (i.e., C | M/4), all live in (ℤ/M)^× via reduction, and a divisor a of some 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod M certainly has a ≡ −1 mod 4C. So: fix M = 4·lcm(1..K); pool all prime factors of 4Cp+1 for C | M/4; if the pooled sequence is long enough (≥ D((ℤ/M)^×)) and generates, EGZ-type theorems give a subset product ≡ −1 mod M — but the subset must come from a SINGLE 4Cp+1 to be a divisor. So pooling doesn't directly help; unless the pooled products correspond to divisors of Π_C (4Cp+1) — which IS a p-tied integer (a polynomial in p of degree K!), with modulus M. So: 'the polynomial P_K(p) = Π_{C|M/4}(4Cp+1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod M' is a necessary-ish consequence… does it imply an ES certificate? A divisor of the product is a product of divisors of the factors; need all of it inside one factor. No. Record as a structured negative: pooling across C breaks the 'single integer' requirement — THIS is B2 in zero-sum language.
why: Shows precisely why zero-sum theory (which handles long sequences) doesn't apply: ES's sequences are short (ω ≈ log log) per integer, and pooling destroys the divisor structure. Clean statement of B2.
first_step: Write it up as a one-paragraph negative in the lane md; no computation needed.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over F₂ for a parity count of certificates
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives #solutions ≡ 0 (mod p) for low-degree systems over F_p; integer analogues count solutions mod 2 via polynomial identities. INVOLUTION_ES / WINDMILL ask for an odd weighted count of ES solutions.
why: It is the algebraic native parity tool. It applies to finite-field point counts, not positive integer points, unless the certificate set is encoded as F₂-points of an auxiliary variety.
first_step: Encode the slot-lemma condition (4 | some pentagon entry) as F₂-variety points of an auxiliary system over (ℤ/2)^k (via binary digits?) and compute counts mod 2 for p < 2000.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0085] Find a polynomial system over F_2 or F_3 whose solution set maps onto ES(p) certificates for p ≤ 10³; check CW degree condition.

title: Cryptographic hardness assumption: 'ES-certificate search is hard' as a one-way function candidate
connection: If certificates were hard to find but easy to verify, p ↦ certificate is a NP-search; crypto reductions require average-case hardness ↔ ES almost-all results suggest easy on average.
why: Fun meta: certificate search is easy heuristically (small C works), so ES gives no OWF; that easiness itself is evidence of a uniform algorithm.
first_step: Quantify: over primes ≤ 10⁹, distribution of the work (number of trials) to find the first certificate; if max work is polylog, conjecture a 'polylog search time' strengthening.

title: Supersaturation: ES certificates as copies of a small 'pattern' in a dense p-dependent structure
connection: Supersaturation (Erdős–Simonovits, Blakley–Roy) yields many copies of a pattern in any dense enough host ↔ define a host structure H_p (e.g. a bipartite graph between u and C with edges for (4uC−1) | p+u...?) — edges are the certificates themselves, so need a pattern built from easier objects.
why: If certificates could be expressed as copies of a pattern in a host whose density is forced (e.g. by divisor counts of an interval), Blakley–Roy-type inequalities give pointwise counts.
first_step: Look for a host graph G_p with ≫ p edges (e.g. pairs (a,b) with ab ≡ 1 mod something tied to p) where a 4-cycle or path of length 2 corresponds to an ES certificate; then apply Sidorenko-type lower bounds.

title: Hypergraph containers for 'certificate-avoiding' factorisation patterns
connection: In the abstract model, a failing p corresponds to an assignment of factorisation patterns to {4Cp+1}_C avoiding every certificate, i.e. an independent set in a certificate hypergraph. The container method (Balogh–Morris–Samotij; Saxton–Thomason) counts independent sets and shows that they lie in few small containers.
why: Containers would give an upper bound on the number of consistent avoiding patterns, which gives exceptional-set bounds via counting, a native extremal-combinatorics route.
first_step: Formalise the hypergraph on (level, residue-class-of-factor) vertices; estimate codegrees and apply the container lemma heuristically to bound the avoiding patterns.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0338] Formulate the hypergraph whose edges are certificate classes; apply container counting to bound evaders up to X (heuristic).

title: Erdős's covering argument for prime plus powers of two
connection: The complement of n=p+2^k is controlled by congruence covering phenomena, resembling ES's finite congruence cover (F03) and thin-family unions (F34).
why: Covering congruences are a direct combinatorial mechanism for proving either coverage or obstruction, relevant to ES's certificate-line cover.
first_step: Write the covering congruence system in the Erdős argument and test whether ES failed primes have a finite modular covering explanation.
refs: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113–123

title: Graceful tree conjecture: infinite families and absorption
connection: Graceful labeling shares F01,F05w,F23,F34: a universal finite-graph existence problem, many verified cases/families, and proof strategies that cover large classes. ES likewise needs an infinite union of thin certificate families.
why: The absorption method may suggest how to ensure a partial family cover can absorb leftover objects rather than merely prove density.
first_step: Read an absorption proof for a tree labeling result and abstract its ‘leave’ and absorber; formulate analogous objects as uncovered ES prime classes and certificate families.

title: Sum-product estimates for reciprocal sets
connection: Reciprocal additive equations share F12, F22, F33 and couple additive structure to multiplication of denominators.
why: Incidence bounds may quantify how many distinct reciprocal sums a structured denominator set can generate.
first_step: Apply an incidence bound to the sets {1/a} and {1/b+1/c} for bounded denominator ranges and compare with required p-scale.

title: Graph connectivity of Diophantine representations
connection: Representation graphs share F14, F38, F39: vertices are solutions and local transformations connect them.
why: If each nonempty fibre has a canonical connected component, induction or descent might extend from a set of seeds.
first_step: Construct the ES witness graph under coordinate swaps and Vieta moves for small primes, then determine whether graph invariants suggest a general connectivity lemma.

title: Burgess-type bounds via Hanson–Petridis Stepanov method for structured residue sets
connection: Hanson–Petridis improve the Paley-graph clique bound to √(p/2)+1 using Stepanov's polynomial method; the repo found χ-product cliques sit in a QR coset and that |A|-only Hoffman/Huang bounds fail below (p−1)/2.
why: Stepanov's method uses more than |A| — multiplicative structure — which is what the χ-product clique obstruction asks for.
first_step: Apply the Hanson–Petridis polynomial to the repo's χ-product clique family and see whether it gives a bound depending on the generating set.
refs: Hanson–Petridis, Refined estimates concerning sumsets contained in the roots of unity, arXiv:1905.09134

title: Kemnitz/Reiher-style lattice-point zero-sum for joint (C, d) conditions
connection: Reiher's Kemnitz theorem concerns zero-sums in (ℤ/n)²; ES certificates require simultaneous congruences (on f mod 4c and mod d), i.e. zero-sums in products of cyclic groups.
why: Multi-dimensional zero-sum constants control simultaneous residue requirements.
first_step: Formulate the Type I certificate condition f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) as a zero-sum in ℤ/4c × ℤ/d of log-classes of prime factors and compute the relevant constant for small c,d.
refs: Reiher, On Kemnitz' conjecture…, Ramanujan J. 13 (2007)

title: Huang sensitivity / interlacing on the ES certificate hypercube
connection: Huang's proof uses a signed adjacency matrix of the hypercube and Cauchy interlacing to force a high-degree vertex in any large induced subgraph; ES certificates live on a product of small 'choice' cubes (choice of prime factors into a,b).
why: Interlacing arguments convert 'large set' into 'has a forced structure' — the repo noted Hoffman/Huang bounds depending only on |A| fail; a signed-matrix variant with the χ structure is still open.
first_step: Construct a signing of the divisor-lattice cube of N such that the eigenvalue bound encodes the class −1 mod e; test numerically on hard primes.

[upgrades-0293] Compute by brute force, for e ≤ 50 and k ≤ 12 with random labels, the maximum certificate-free subset family size.

title: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune restricted sumsets for distinct-factor products
connection: Erdős–Heilbronn (Dias da Silva–Hamidoune): |h^∧A| ≥ min(p, h|A| − h² + 1) for restricted h-fold sums in ℤ/p; ES uses products of distinct prime factors (restricted products).
why: Exact lower bounds for restricted product sets in cyclic groups of prime order (take discrete logs mod e−1 when e−1 is prime-ish).
first_step: Compute restricted product set sizes of prime factors of N mod e and compare with the DdS–H bound.
refs: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune, Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory, Bull. LMS 26 (1994)

title: Matrix-tree theorem with signed/twisted weights: the ES sign as a determinant of a twisted Laplacian
connection: (A/p) for the fan graph equals the Legendre symbol of a principal cofactor of the reduced Laplacian M (principal cofactors of the full Laplacian all equal p). Twisted Laplacians (connection Laplacians with ℤ/2 or ℤ/4 holonomy) compute signed spanning-forest counts (Kenyon's cycle-rooted spanning forests).
why: Kenyon's vector-bundle Laplacian theory computes topological invariants of forests via determinants. A ℤ/4 connection might encode the slot-lemma condition '4 | some pentagon entry'.
first_step: Put a ℤ/4 connection on the fan graph; compute det of the connection Laplacian and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all words for p < 1000.
refs: Kenyon, Spanning forests and the vector bundle Laplacian (Ann. Probab. 2011)

title: Laurent phenomenon: all frieze entries as Laurent polynomials in an initial seed (c, m) with coefficient N
connection: In a cluster algebra with frozen N, every entry is a Laurent polynomial in an initial cluster. ES words are integrality (positivity) points of these Laurent polynomials, so ES₅ is an 'integer specialisation of a cluster algebra' problem.
why: The theory of integer points of cluster varieties (positivity, theta bases, Fock–Goncharov) is native here, and may give parametrisations of all words by a seed.
first_step: Write the five entries as Laurent polynomials in (c,m) with N; the integrality condition is (cm−1) | (N + c). Record that the frieze reproduces the hyperbola/divisor condition, and check whether any other seed gives a different divisor condition.

title: Kasteleyn/Pfaffian orientations: ES count as a Pfaffian of a skew matrix built from p
connection: Perfect matchings of planar graphs are Pfaffians. Windmill-type 'odd number of fixed points' arguments are mod-2 Pfaffian/determinant arguments. A planar graph G_p with ES certificates as matchings would give #certificates = |Pf(K_p)|.
why: Exact Pfaffian formulas give closed-form counts, and nonvanishing of a determinant is checkable algebraically (e.g. via its value mod a prime).
first_step: Attempt to realise the forest F_p's edges or the words as perfect matchings of a planar graph; compute det mod 2 for small p.

title: Sperner / KKM / Tucker lemmas for a labelled triangulation whose 'rainbow cell' is a certificate
connection: Sperner's lemma gives an odd number of fully labelled simplices. If the triangle {x+y+z = const} or the (u,v) quadrant can be triangulated with labels from p-arithmetic (e.g. Legendre symbols and divisibility), a rainbow cell might encode a word with the right sign.
why: It is the combinatorial-topology native parity engine with geometric flexibility. The forest bichromatic-edge statement is already a 1-dimensional Sperner-type statement (path from QR to QNR has a bichromatic edge).
first_step: Write the 1-D Sperner argument behind H4/forest bichromatic edges explicitly; then look for a 2-D labelling that encodes the extra divisibility.

title: Lorenzini's critical-polynomial question (W) and the A₃ graph: I3 as a sandpile statement
connection: LORENZINI_W: (W) asks that every n outside a finite set is xyz − x − z (x,y,z ≥ 2), which comes from critical groups of A₃-type graphs. I3 (t,u,v ≥ 3) is a strengthening.
why: This is the graph-theory native home of I3. Lorenzini's and Wang–Lu's density-1 results are its nearest theorems.
first_step: Check Wang–Lu (EJC 2026) methods for density 1 and whether they extend to the I3 lower bound t,u,v ≥ 3 (repo has an unconditional rate).
refs: Wang–Lu, The critical polynomials of simple connected graphs, EJC 33(3) (2026)

title: Tutte polynomial of the fan graph: evaluations beyond T(1,1) = p
connection: The fan multigraph's Tutte polynomial T(x,y) has T(1,1) = p. Other evaluations count forests, acyclic orientations, recurrent sandpile levels (Merino) and, via Thistlethwaite, the Jones polynomial of the associated alternating link.
why: It is a single polynomial carrying graph, sandpile and knot data. The ES sign might be an evaluation (e.g. T(−1,−1) or a root-of-unity value).
first_step: Compute T(x,y) symbolically for the fan in terms of (t,u,v) and evaluate at small roots of unity; correlate with the slot-lemma sign.

title: Temperley bijection: ES₅ fan ↔ a planar bipartite graph with exactly p perfect matchings
connection: Temperley's bijection maps spanning trees of a planar graph G to perfect matchings of a derived bipartite graph. The fan multigraph with τ = p therefore yields a planar bipartite graph with p dimer configurations; Kasteleyn matrices compute them as determinants, and height functions carry signs.
why: Dimer models have height functions and Kasteleyn signs; the ES sign (pairing class) might be a dimer observable, e.g. the parity of height-function flux around a face.
first_step: Construct the Temperley graph of the fan for small words and compute the Kasteleyn matrix; test whether a height-function statistic mod 2 matches the slot-lemma sign.

title: Slice-rank bounds for certificate-avoiding exponent sets
connection: Croot–Lev–Pach/Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound sets avoiding x + y + z = 0 via slice rank. ES failure constrains the exponent vectors (mod 2, or in the character group) of prime factors of N_e so that no ±1 combination hits the class of −1: a linear-avoidance condition in a 2-group quotient of (ℤ/e)*. Slice-rank-type bounds limit such sets.
why: Gives quantitative 'avoidance is rare' statements in elementary abelian quotients of (ℤ/e)*.
first_step: For e with (ℤ/e)*/squares ≅ F₂^r, formulate the avoidance condition on the F₂-vectors of prime factors and compute the maximal avoiding sets for small r.
refs: arXiv:1605.01506 (Croot-Lev-Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small)

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz on the trial form
connection: Alon's nullstellensatz proves existence of a nonvanishing point in a grid. R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d(p) | d + 1, d² ≤ 4c_d(p)p + 1}: encode 'no d in a grid of structured values works' as a polynomial vanishing on a product set, and look for a monomial whose coefficient is nonzero.
why: A purely algebraic existence argument; most likely to work in a finite-field shadow (mod q) of the problem, giving at least a structural lemma.
first_step: Formulate the mod-q shadow: for prime q, find (u, C) ∈ S₁ × S₂ (small sets) with 4uC − 1 ≡ 0 and p + u ≡ 0 (mod q); test the nullstellensatz coefficient condition.

title: Erdős–Selfridge distinct-small-parts mechanism for consecutive levels
connection: Erdős–Selfridge: writing consecutive factors as a_i·(power) forces the a_i to be distinct and small, contradiction by counting. ES failure forces each 4Cp+1 (C = 1, …, K) into a thin multiplicative set S_C; write 4Cp+1 = a_C·b_C with b_C the S_C-compatible part and look for a forced-distinctness/smallness contradiction among the a_C.
why: An elementary combinatorial mechanism for consecutive terms that might bite on the explicit sets S_C at small C.
first_step: For C ≤ 8 characterise S_C explicitly (e.g. S_1: all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) and test numerically how small K can be such that no prime has 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K... (there are such primes for each K; record their density decay).

title: Min-plus 'ES': n/4 = min-plus harmonic combination — degenerate, records the archimedean bound
connection: Tropicalizing at ∞ (log-sizes) gives max(−log x, −log y, −log z) = log(4/n) up to O(1): just the size bound x ≍ n. So the tropical-at-∞ world only records sizes, confirming that the archimedean information is the size window.
why: Clarifies that all non-trivial content is non-archimedean + integrality; the archimedean place contributes only 'x ∈ (n/4, 3n/4]'.
first_step: Context lemma; no computation needed.

title: Between: Smooth-denominator ES
connection: Require x, y, z to be y-smooth (y = (log p)^A). The count drops with A; find the A where failures start.
why: Gives a tunable count family inside ES; the critical A tells how much 'slack' ES has.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10^6 the minimal smoothness bound of the best solution; fit vs log p.

connection: The least common denominator of a solution of 4/n is divisible by n except exactly when 4 | n (data n ≤ 30 000; OEIS A008586 match for the exception positions).

connection: Without the n ≡ 1 (4) restriction, U-zeros are mostly even (multiples of 4 with n+1 prime-ish); non-OEIS.

title: Isosceles solutions (two equal denominators) exist at a prime iff p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (or p = 2)
connection: The primes ≤ 10⁵ with no solution having x = y or y = z are exactly the 4 783 primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) (OEIS first-20 match: A002144 Pythagorean primes); composite failures ≤ 3000 start 25, 65, 85, … (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4?).

title: Integer programming with witness cuts
connection: Use integer programming on a linearized auxiliary formulation, adding exact cuts learned from failed modular assignments.
why: A solver can discover useful constraints while all final witnesses remain directly checkable.
first_step: Linearize one bounded factor-allocation model and add only cuts proved from its congruence equations.

title: Fair interleaving of infinite families
connection: Run countably many valid parameter searches in a schedule that eventually explores every finite parameter tuple.
why: Fairness prevents one expensive family from starving other methods, without guaranteeing ES itself.

title: Stopping bounds for ordered triples

connection: Certificate search is bottlenecked by factoring p-tied integers; ES only needs some divisor in a class, so partial factorisation (ECM to bound B) suffices for most C.

connection: e-slice success is a subset-product problem: choose a sub-multiset of prime factors of N whose product ratio is −1 mod e; with ω(N) small, brute force is trivial, but for highly composite N or pooled factors it's subset-sum in ℤ/(e−1) (discrete logs).

title: Lenstra integer programming in fixed dimension for 'certificate in a box' decisions

title: Naive parity of a level count is trivial — record the lemma and the needed asymmetry
connection: D_t^−(tp+1) is even unless tp+1 = s² with s ≡ −1 (mod t), i.e. unless p = t − 2; so parity of single-level counts carries no information (pairing d ↔ N/d). Zagier needed an asymmetric second involution.
why: Clears a trap: any parity proof needs a set where the obvious involution is broken (e.g. by a non-symmetric constraint like d < N/d with an extra condition).

connection: ES₅ says ES ⇔ λ(p) ≤ 3 for a continued-fraction length. In F_q[T], Zaremba-type statements (all partial quotients of degree 1) are known for small q; the length-3 statement is a much weaker FF analogue.

connection: Zaremba (Bourgain–Kontorovich; claimed in full by Zhang 2605.02518) bounds digits; ES₅ bounds length with unbounded digits. The 'dual Zaremba' problem, existence of A with r(p/A) ≤ L in a prescribed coset, is the ES form.

To supply it one could: nothing to supply; instead PROVE formally that ES failure sets cannot be cut out by finitely many congruences beyond T1 (B1-type lemma, already partly known)

title: O(n) is odd ⟺ n ≡ 2 (mod 4) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000 (S₃-orbit parity)
connection: Ordered count = #(x=y=z) + 3·#(exactly two equal) + 6·#(distinct), so O(n) ≡ #(all equal) + #(two equal) (mod 2); in range this is odd exactly for n ≡ 2 (mod 4) (the OEIS hit A121262 for 'O mod 2' was an offset artefact of starting at n = 2). Also O(n) ≢ 0 (mod 6) ⟺ n even (in range).
why: Parity of a count via its degenerate (isosceles/equilateral) solutions is the 'involution' template of WINDMILL.md; here the degenerate solutions are fully classified by the isosceles factorisation (see the isosceles-law item), so the parity law should be provable.
first_step: Prove the n ≡ 2 (mod 4) law by counting isosceles solutions via (4x−2n)(4z−n) = 2n² and (4x−n)(4z−2n) = 2n² and the equilateral one (3n/4 integral); then look for a finer involution on U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) (where there are no degenerate solutions).

connection: Every n in range has an ES solution with x | y (share 0.14 of solutions); 4/n − 1/z = (k+1)/(kx) means 4/n − 1/z = a/b (lowest terms) with b having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod a).
why: x | y is the 'divisor ≡ −1 (mod a)' event again — equivalent in spirit to the word families (tuv − u − v); a direct bridge between the Egyptian-fraction shape and the word/U formulation.
first_step: Write the bijection between x | y solutions and words n = tuv − u − v (or a sub-family) and compare counts.

title: Distinct-only count D(p) = U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4); U(p) − D(p) = 2 exactly at every prime p ≡ 3 (4), p > 7
connection: Verified over all primes ≤ 2·10⁵: U − D = 0 at all 8 977 primes ≡ 1 (4) and U − D = 2 at all 9 004 primes ≡ 3 (4) > 7 — the two isosceles solutions predicted by the factorisations (4x−2p)(4z−p) = 2p² and (4x−p)(4z−2p) = 2p².
why: Exact corollary of the proved isosceles law: the distinct and non-distinct ES problems coincide on the hard class, and the orbit-size correction O(p) − 6D(p) is an explicit constant at p ≡ 3 (4).

connection: ES₅ ⟺ a certain rational has continued-fraction length λ ≤ 3. Thermodynamic formalism (Mayer transfer operator, Bowen's formula) controls the distribution of CF lengths over rationals with given denominator.

connection: Repo mentions SL₂ words. Membership-in-product-set problems in SL₂(ℤ) are decidable (automaticity of SL₂) and have automaton-theoretic structure; the 'length ≤ 3' condition of ES₅ is a bounded word length.

connection: Repo's I3 is the untied version (any t ≥ 3); ES needs t ∈ 4ℤ. The gap between 'some t ≥ 3' (proved for all large n? or census only?) and 't ≡ 0 mod 4' is a *congruence condition on one parameter* — maybe the I3 mechanism can be twisted by a character.

connection: The set W = {(C, a) : a ≡ −1 mod 4C} has density 0 in ℕ² but positive 'logarithmic' density along C; ES says the map p ↦ (p mod a) hits a prescribed class in W for every p. Furstenberg's correspondence turns density into recurrence; multiple recurrence (Szemerédi-type) gives patterns in every positive-density set but says nothing about one specific p.
why: Probably a dead end, but 'ES for all p' resembles 'recurrence for every point' = topological dynamics (minimal systems), where pointwise results (Birkhoff, Hindman) exist. Is the ES certificate set a return-time set of a minimal system?

connection: Conway's rational tangles are classified by their fraction p/A, and tangle operations (twist, rotate) act as SL₂(ℤ)/PSL₂ moves. ES₅ asks for a tangle with a 3-vertex linear-plumbing (negative-CF) description (not an 'even' CF; twist-region conventions differ) whose fraction's denominator is a non-residue mod p.

title: Analogy of analogy: ES ↔ Zaremba ↔ Markoff ↔ Apollonian — the 'thin orbit' quadrilateral; where does ES sit in the (orbit, expansion, obstruction) triangle?
connection: Zaremba (solved, claimed): thin semigroup orbit, expansion, no obstruction. Markoff mod p: group orbit, expansion, divisibility rigidity. Apollonian: thin group orbit, expansion, reciprocity obstruction (local-global FALSE). ES: no known group/semigroup, polylog count, reciprocity obstruction at squares. The missing ingredient is the orbit; the free-lane question: can ES certificates be realised as a thin *semigroup* orbit in SL₂(ℤ) or in a 2×2×2 cube structure, with p as a 'level'?
why: Pattern-matching across the four problems isolates exactly one missing ingredient (an orbit structure) — a concrete target for construction rather than proof.
first_step: Write the ES₅ CF form as a product of SL₂(ℤ) generators (Zaremba-style: p/q with partial quotients ≤ A ⟺ matrix in a semigroup orbit); identify what plays the role of 'q' and whether ES is 'λ ≤ 3' for a rational with *p-tied* numerator — then it's a *level* condition, not an orbit condition. Document the mismatch precisely.

title: Bourgain–Kontorovich-style 'local-global for a thin semigroup orbit' in the C-direction: fix p, vary (u, v): p = 4Cuv − u − v
connection: Rewrite p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟹ for fixed C this is a quadratic form in (u, v) (indefinite: 4Cuv − u − v); p is represented by the 'form' Q_C(u,v) = 4Cuv − u − v for some C. Representation of p by one of a family of indefinite binary quadratic polynomials — a family of *quadratic* problems, each with a class-group structure (indefinite forms: Pell-type unit group acts on representations!).
why: For fixed C, representations of p by 4Cuv − u − v: complete the square: (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1; so it's the divisor problem again — but the INDEFINITE FORM viewpoint says: the 'automorphs' of the form act on solutions; the form 4Cuv − u − v has discriminant (4C)² — a *square* discriminant, so the form is degenerate (a product of linear forms) and its automorph group is trivial. OK so no Pell action — that's why no orbit. Document: 'the ES form has square discriminant; its automorph group is trivial; hence no Vieta/Pell dynamics'. This is a clean statement of the missing orbit.
first_step: Write it up as a lemma: every ES parametrisation (Type I, Type II, e-slice) has a quadratic form of square discriminant ⟹ no infinite automorphism group ⟹ no orbit dynamics. Check Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd — discriminant of the relevant form is −16c²d, NOT square — so Type I does have a class group (finite, ℚ(√−d)) but no infinite unit group. So the only rigid structure is the finite class group of ℚ(√−d), varying with d.

title: Type I as a Frobenius-type formula? Look for a semigroup interpretation of the Type I parametrisation
connection: Type II (★) is a 2-generator k-Frobenius identity ↔ Type I (f | p² + 4c²d …) may correspond to a different invariant (e.g. Frobenius number of ⟨a, b, c⟩ or genus of ⟨u,v⟩: genus = (u−1)(v−1)/2).
why: If Type I also has a semigroup meaning, ES would be 'p is one of a few semigroup invariants of some small semigroup' — a uniform language for all certificates.
first_step: Write the Type I solution family in ET variables and test whether p equals g_t, genus, or other standard invariants (e.g. number of gaps, conductor) of ⟨·,·⟩ with parameters from the solution.

title: IMO 2007/5 Vieta jumping (4ab−1 | (4a²−1)² ⇒ a = b) as an involution proof of T1-type statements
connection: The IMO problem is the same form 4ab − 1 as level-4 ES divisors (d ≡ −1 mod 4). Its standard solution is Vieta jumping (infinite descent on an involution orbit).
why: Vieta-jumping proofs give a dynamical (descent) proof of non-existence; reversing the descent (ascent) is a way to generate witnesses — F38. Note the ES word itself is multilinear (degree 1 in each variable), so the Vieta involution lives on an auxiliary quadratic, as in the IMO solution.
first_step: Identify the auxiliary quadratic in the IMO solution ((4a²−1)² = k(4ab−1), quadratic in a) whose Vieta involution proves the level-4 statement, and write its analogue for level 4C divisors d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cm²+1.

title: Continued-fraction convergence bounds for word certificates
connection: The continuant estimates in arXiv:2106.03789 concern extremal sizes of structured continued fractions, matching ES F17/F32 and the small-witness feature F04's sparse-count setting.
why: Size bounds can test whether a word construction has polynomial-size denominators, a prerequisite for a useful ES certificate family.
first_step: Read the extremal bound and apply it to length-three ES words with the required coordinate congruences; record the resulting denominator exponent.

title: Bounded continued-fraction words and thin ES families
connection: The extremal continuant results in arXiv:2106.03789 match ES F17/F30/F32: restricted words generate thin infinite families with controlled growth, analogous to known ES families that do not yet cover all primes.
why: It offers estimates for the cost and density of one certificate family without treating thinness as a reason to discard it.
first_step: Apply the paper's extremal bounds to an ES word family such as periodic partial quotients and estimate the number of primes it could cover up to X.

title: Zaremba: thin semigroup growth versus universal coverage
connection: Zaremba shares F01, F17, F22, F30: universal denominator coverage is conjectured, while restricted-CF semigroups first yield large/thin sets. ES similarly has thin proved prime families but no all-prime rung (F30).
why: Growth and expansion estimates for a structured thin set may suggest how to move from infinitely many ES prime families toward density or coverage.
first_step: Extract the precise denominator-count lower bound in the cited paper and ask whether a corresponding count of ES primes covered by bounded parameter boxes is accessible.

title: Zaremba feature flip: bounded partial quotients
connection: Zaremba matches ES’s universal-existence goal, matrix/continued-fraction structure, and computational checks (F01,F18,F23), but demands bounded partial quotients (F17w) rather than ES’s bounded CF length. This feature-flip isolates a stronger regularity condition.
why: Understanding what bounded digits buy—expansion and uniformity—could identify which ES CF constraints are essential versus convenient.
first_step: Compare the matrix products in Zaremba’s proof with ES₅ matrices and record exactly where a uniform digit bound enters.

title: Numerical semigroup Apéry sets and finite residue certificates
connection: The Frobenius problem shares F03,F10,F32: congruence classes modulo a generator reduce an infinite additive semigroup question to finite residue representatives. ES witness divisibility similarly reduces to residue classes and a finite certificate.
why: Apéry-set bookkeeping is a concrete way to ensure residue coverage is complete rather than heuristic.
first_step: For small primes, tabulate ES’s admissible divisors by residue class modulo 4C and compare the completeness proof format with Apéry-set closure.

title: SL₂ word problem: continued fractions as matrix products
connection: Restricted continued fractions and SL₂ words share F16w,F17,F18,F32: a finite digit string is a short certificate for a matrix entry. ES’s length-three negative-continuant representation is unusually short, suggesting direct word enumeration.
why: Canonical word forms and reversal symmetries could reduce redundant ES parametrizations and reveal missing congruence types.
first_step: Derive ES’s negative-continuant matrix product explicitly and test the standard continued-fraction normalization on small prime cases.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Continued fractions and bounded-length Diophantine representations
connection: Bounded continued-fraction problems share F16, F17, F32 and encode integers through short recurrences.
why: Short-CF classification may produce new finite families of ES certificates or expose the exact exceptional parameter set.
first_step: Translate the ES₅ formulation into continuants and search for a theorem bounding the omitted length-three cases.

title: Orbit counting under S3 symmetry
connection: Symmetric representation problems share F14, F38, F04; orbit-stabilizer corrections affect the count of witnesses.
why: Correctly separating generic and degenerate orbits may improve exact counting and parity deductions.
first_step: Compute stabilizers of ES triples and derive an orbit-count identity for R(p), including repeated-coordinate cases.

title: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang polynomially effective unipotent equidistribution
connection: LMW (2022) give polynomially effective equidistribution for one-parameter unipotent orbits in SL₂(ℝ)×SL₂(ℝ)/Γ and SL₂(ℂ)/Γ-type spaces; ES Type II solutions are SL₂(ℤ) matrices [[f,a],[b,f′]] with ab = 4c²dp and f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd), i.e. lattice points in a thin region of SL₂.
why: Effective rates are the prerequisite for counting lattice points in shrinking/thin regions (polylog many expected).
first_step: Write the Type II count as a count of Γ₀(4cd)-points in a region of SL₂(ℝ) depending on p and estimate its volume vs LMW error terms.
refs: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang, Effective equidistribution for some one parameter unipotent flows, arXiv:2211.11099

title: Casson–Walker invariant / Dedekind sum of L(p,A) restricted to HJ-length-3 A
connection: λ_CW(L(p,q)) is a Dedekind sum s(q,p) up to normalisation, and Rademacher-type congruences tie 12p·s(q,p) mod 8 to (q/p). On words, s(A,p) has a closed form in (t,u,v) by Dedekind reciprocity.
why: It gives an explicit integer-valued topological invariant of the word whose residue mod 8 is the ES sign. Sums over words then become sums of a topological invariant.
first_step: Derive s(tu−1, p) in closed form from three applications of reciprocity; compare with DEDEKIND_ES §4.

title: Closed horocycle at height 1/p: equidistribution of (a + i)/p and cusp excursions
connection: Every closed horocycle of length → ∞ equidistributes (Sarnak/Hejhal; sparse versions by Venkatesh, Strömbergsson). Points (a + i)/p, a mod p, lift ES₅-type continued-fraction data of a/p; ES₅ needs a point whose cusp excursion has a specific deep shape.
why: Puts ES₅ into the horocycle-equidistribution world where every-p statements exist — but probably at too deep a cusp scale (B2), which this item would quantify.
first_step: Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into a statement on the cusp depth/shape of some (a + i)/p and compare with the scales reachable by effective equidistribution.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0040] Compute the measure of the 'HJ-length ≤ 3' cusp region in the unit tangent bundle; compare with the count |L₃(p)| ≈ log²p to see the scale.
refs: Strömbergsson, On the uniform equidistribution of long closed horocycles (Duke 2004)

title: Vallée's dynamical analysis of Euclidean algorithms (by-excess algorithm) with a quadratic character
connection: The HJ expansion is the 'by-excess' Euclidean algorithm. Vallée's transfer-operator method gives limit laws for costs such as length. ES₅ asks for the extreme value: min length over A in the non-residue class equals 3.
why: It is the native analysis-of-algorithms framework; twisting transfer operators by Dirichlet characters is done in Baladi–Vallée-type works.
first_step: Look up whether the by-excess algorithm's length distribution has been studied with a character twist (Baladi–Vallée 2005 for Gauss map; Dolgopyat estimates).

title: Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1} on X(1) × X(1) and ES words as its points with level structure
connection: Pairs of lattices with cyclic isogeny of degree N_t = tp+1 form the modular curve X₀(N_t). A word is a factorisation N_t = A·A* with congruences mod t, which is a Γ₀/Γ₁-level datum.
why: It gives ES₅ a moduli interpretation: level-t structures on isogenies of degree tp + 1. Moduli-theoretic counts (Riemann–Hurwitz on X₀) are exact.
first_step: Write the bijection {words of level t} ↔ {points on a specified cover of X₀(N_t) over ℤ}; check whether the sign is a Galois/Atkin–Lehner action.

title: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot: words as non-intersecting lattice path families with determinant tuv−u−v
connection: det M(t,u,v) can be read as a signed count of path systems in a planar network (LGV). If the planar network can be chosen so that the count is non-negative termwise, the cofactor A and its class get a path interpretation.
why: LGV gives combinatorial meaning to determinants and cofactors, the same objects as the ES sign (cofactor A mod p). Positivity of path counts is automatic.
first_step: Construct the planar network whose LGV matrix is M(t,u,v); interpret A = tu−1 as a path count and the slot-lemma 4-divisibility as a parity/symmetry of path families.
